report.source_text: Histopathological examination of the descending colon biopsy demonstrated dual morphologies in which a predominant component comprised of tumor cells arranged in nested, organoid, and rosette-like growth patterns with a focal area of solid sheet associated with brisk mitotic activity estimated at 30 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields (Figure 3A). The second minor component (30%) exhibited intermingled malignant glandular structures morphologically consistent with adenocarcinoma (Figure 3B). The predominant component was diffusely positive for Pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and Synaptophysin and negative for Chromogranin immunohisto-chemical stains, whereas adenocarcinoma was negative for the neuroendocrine markers (Figure 3C, 3D).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 48-year-old man with a history of diabetes and ulcerative colitis presented with moderate right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, fatigue, constipation, and significant weight loss (18 kg over 1 month), along with a palpable epigastric mass. Initial lab work was normal. A CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed circumferential wall thickening in the proximal descending colon, regional lymph nodes, multiple peritoneal deposits, and innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses, indicating widespread metastatic disease. Histopathological examination of a descending colon biopsy showed dual morphologies: a predominant neuroendocrine component (positive for Pancytokeratin and Synaptophysin, brisk mitotic activity) and a minor adenocarcinoma component. Based on these radiological and histopathological findings, the patient was diagnosed with metastatic poorly differentiated MANEC of the colon, which was deemed unresectable, with metastases to the liver and multiple peritoneal deposits.

CT scan revealed multiple peritoneal deposits (largest 4.9x3 cm) and innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses in both liver lobes (largest 8.1 cm at segment 4b), confirming metastatic disease to the peritoneum and liver.
CT scan also showed necrotic lymphadenopathy at the gastrohepatic ligament.

Histopathological examination of the descending colon biopsy demonstrated dual morphologies: a predominant component with neuroendocrine features (nested, organoid, rosette-like growth, solid sheet, brisk mitotic activity of 30 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, positive for Pancytokeratin and Synaptophysin, negative for Chromogranin) and a minor component (30%) consistent with adenocarcinoma (negative for neuroendocrine markers).
The patient was diagnosed with metastatic poorly differentiated MANEC of the colon, which was deemed unresectable.
